A female character in this play negotiates for a "mountainy ram" and a load of dung as the price for seducing a man, but she later offers that price to the man if she helps him win a different girl. One character in this play refuses to stay in a building alone with his fiancée because he's scared of what the unseen Father Reilly would say. In this play, a character hired as the new pot-boy is recognized by another character after he wins a mule race. In this play, Shawn Keogh is granted special dispensation to marry Pegeen Mike, who's more interested in a character who smashed someone else in the head with a loy. The 1907 premiere of this play led to riots centered at the Abbey Theatre. Christy Mahon's story about killing his own father earns the admiration of the inhabitants of an Irish village in what play by J.M. Synge?
The Playboy of the Western World

In one poem, this author wrote: "Writing is a puppy biting nothingness / Writing wounds without a trace of blood". The speakers of that poem by him stand "Close to the gardens of broken shadow", where they "cultivate hope". The lines "This is your name-- / a woman said, / and vanished through the winding of a corridor" opens one section of a poem by him that includes the refrain "One day I shall become what I want". The speaker of one poem by this author repeatedly mentions that he has eight children, that he has "a name without a title", and asks "So will you be angry?". That poem by this author of the volumes Mural and State of Siege ends "Beware / Beware / Of my hunger / And my anger" and opens "Write down! / I am an Arab". Name this author of "Identity Card", a Palestinian poet.

A French nobleman in this novel sprays his crops with bull semen in an attempt to produce "milk grass" and has a theory that the earth produces a toxic gas called fludium letale. During a fireworks display in celebration of the king, this novel's protagonist tracks a red-headed girl who is slicing plums and strangles her to death. That protagonist of this novel holes himself up in a mountain for seven years after discovering that substances like glass and hair cannot have their essences distilled in an alembic. After apprenticing with Giuseppe Baldini, the protagonist of this novel becomes a serial killer of adolescent virgins in the town of Grasse, in order to manufacture a scent that will make people love him. Jean- Bapstise Grenouille is the murderous, smell-obsessed protagonist of what novel by Patrick Süskind?

A professor in this novel bores people at a party by trying to explain his namesake hypothesis about the historical significance of Pittsburgh. In this novel, a cat that destroys the pigskin briefcase of its owner's new boyfriend is sent to a psychiatrist. That cat's owner and her boyfriend meet when the man's sculptor ex-girlfriend takes out a personal ad for him without his consent. One character in this novel is arrested at an anti-nuclear protest at Lungelss Labs. That one-time lover of a gay Catholic man named Ed, who owns a pet iguana named Arnold Schwarzenegger, marries the iguana owner's sister, Liz Dorati, who spends most of the novel dating John. This work uses a sonnet form inspired by Pushkin's Eugene Onegin. Name this novel in verse about yuppies in 1980's San Francisco, by Vikram Seth.

This poem is the subject of "Miniaturizing, Modeling, and Mocking Ideas", the first chapter of Helen Vendler's Poets Thinking. In this poem, Vice is described as a monster whom when we become "familiar with her face / We first endure, then pity, then embrace." The subject of this poem is described as "Created half to rise, and half to fall'" and "The glory, jest, and riddle of the world". The first epistle of this poem concludes that in "spite of pride, in erring reason's spite / One truth is clear, Whatever is, is right." This poem opens "Awake, my St. John! Leave all meaner things / To low ambition, and the pride of kings". Its most famous section commands: "Know thyself and presume not God to scan", before explaining what is "The proper study of mankind". Name this poem about the place of human beings in the world by Alexander Pope.

One character in this play says to her gravely ill husband: "Where love is great, the littlest doubts are fear; / Where little fears grow great, great love grows there", and promises she will never remarry by declaring: "A second time I kill my husband dead / When second husband kisses me in bed." The protagonist of this play is killed in a conspiracy between his wife, Baptista, and his nephew, Lucianus. The actors are warned not to saw the air too much with their hands, and to speak their speeches trippingly on the tongue, before performing this play, whose title character dies from having poison poured in his ear. A man who writes a new speech for this play re-titles it The Mousetrap. One member of the audience for this play says "The lady doth protest too much, methinks". Name this play-within-a-play that is staged to reveal Claudius' guilt at the behest of Hamlet.

In this novel, a ski jumper named Nils tries to rape Libby after she responds by quoting Raleigh's "The Nymph's Reply to the Shepherd" when he tries to seduce her by reading her "The Passionate Shepherd to His Love." In this novel, Gus LeRoy has an affair with Polly but eventually returns to his wife, in part because he promised his wife to undergo psychoanalysis. Other characters in this novel include Priss Hartshorn, who debates whether to breastfeed her son, and Dottie Renfrew, who is deflowered by an arrogant artist named Dick Brown. This novel begins with the marriage of the unsuccessful playwright Harald Petersen to Kay Strong, and ends with Kay's funeral. Taking place in the 1930s, it follows the lives of eight friends who graduated from Vassar. Name this novel by Mary McCarthy.

This character is the subject of a laudatory song which describes him as a "hunter with eyeballs of flame" after asking "Who has delivered us, who?" At the beginning of the story in which he appears, this character nearly drowns, but is saved by a boy named Teddy. This character kills Karait, and is warned by Chuchundra that he may be in danger. In Man and Superman, Ann's nickname for Octavius is a pun on this character's name. In a climactic scene, he follows an enemy into her underground lair, and emerges victorious after a lengthy battle. This character, whose name derives from his war cry, is an ally of the tailor bird Darzee, and his nemeses are Nag and Nagaina, a pair of cobras. Name this brave mongoose from Rudyard Kipling's The Jungle Book.

The speaker of this poem describes her lover clasping her "aching, melting, unafraid" after chasing her through a maze. One character in this poem "had a whim that sunlight carried blessing," although the speaker of this poem takes refuge from the heat of the sun in the shade of a lime tree. The speaker of this poem wears a stiff brocade and a dress with a pink and silver train, and she makes note of the daffodils and squills blowing in the wind. This poem, which was published in the collection Men, Women and Ghosts, ends by asking "Christ! What are [the title things] for?" It describes the speaker walking "down the garden paths" after receiving a letter informing her that her fiancée Lord Hartwell has been killed in action. Name this anti-war poem by Amy Lowell.

The protagonist of this novel has a therapist named Rena who is a Santeria priestess. A coal salesman in this novel is beaten by a paramilitary officer after stepping on his foot, and is later murdered. This novel begins with its protagonist making a Mother's Day card with a dried daffodil in it for her aunt. The narrator of this novel invents a man named Henry Napoleon to avoid telling her mother that she is in love with her neighbor Joseph, with whom she has a daughter named Brigitte. Several characters in this novel are regularly tested for virginity by their mothers. The narrator's mother Martine is haunted by the rape she suffered as a young woman in the cane fields, and the narrator lives with her mother in New York and with Tante Atie in Haiti. Name this novel about Sophie Caco by Edwidge Danticat.

In Arabic poetry, the equivalent of this genre is known as naqa'id. A work in this genre by Patrick Hume of Polwarth and Alexander Montgomerie contributed to the latter's ascension to the leadership of the Castalian Band. The earliest surviving example of this genre from Scotland is called Sir John the Rose, and it features the makars William Dunbar and Walter Kennedy. In a famous scene in this specific genre, a character boasts that he killed nin e sea monsters after another character criticizes his decision to have a swimming contest with Breca. That exchange takes place between Unferth and the title character of Beowulf. The most noted example of this genre in Norse literature is probably the Lokasenna. Name this genre which, much like modern rap battles, consists of the exchange of poetic insults.

One part of this tale has been called the "hissing stanza" because of the sibilance of its lines, such as when a character decries the singing "of such sentence which is against your law's reverence." The narrator of this tale weeps at the death of a small mouse, and swears to Saint Loy. At the end of this tale, the protagonist is compared to Little Saint Hugh of Lincoln, who suffered a similar fate. In this tale, the body of a young boy miraculously starts to sing the hymn "Alma Redemptionis Mater" and doesn't stop until a grain is removed from his tongue. This tale, which opens with an invocation to the Virgin Mary, is told by Madame Eglantine, who wears a brooch with the motto "Amor vincit omnia." In this tale, some Jews are hanged for murdering a boy at the behest of Satan. Name this rather anti-Semitic section of The Canterbury Tales.

This poem predicts an ignominious fate for "he who mocks the infant's faith" and "he who shall teach the child to doubt." One couplet from this poem, which was published separately by the poet with a slightly different wording, describes how "the caterpillar on the leaf reminds thee of thy mother's grief." The Doors' song "End of the Night" quotes this poem's lines about how "some are born to sweet delight" while "some are born to endless night." This poem declares that "a robin redbreast in a cage puts all heaven in a rage." This poem, which consists largely of a litany of paradoxes, begins "To see a world in a grain of sand and a heaven in a wild flower, hold infinity in the palm of your hand, and eternity in an hour." name this poem by William Blake.

One stanza of this poem describes "dead sons from the war" and "daughters whom life had crushed" as well as "their children fatherless, crying." One character in this poem is a major who "had talked with venerable men of the revolution," while another is a fiddler who "played with life all his ninety years, braving the sleet with bared breast." That character babbles "of the horse-races of long ago at Clary's Grove" and "of what Abe Lincoln said one time at Springfield." Two stanzas of this poem list the manners of death of various characters, including one who "was brought to her little space by Ella and Kate and Mag." It begins by asking "Where are Elmer, Herman, Bert, Tom and Charley?" and responding that "all, all are sleeping on" the title location. Name this poem which introduces Edgar Lee Masters' Spoon River Anthology.

Many people have interpreted Dostoevsky's short story "The Crocodile" as satirizing the writing of this novel. In this novel, the medical student Lopukhov enters into a marriage of convenience with a woman who later marries her true love, who shares his name with Turgenev's character Kirsanov. That woman, Vera Pavlovna, is aided by the "extraordinary man" Rakhmetov, and imagines a socialist utopia in her so-called "fourth dream." That dream's imagery of the Crystal Palace is referenced by Dostoevsky's Underground Man. The fourth chapter of Nabokov's The Gift is a biography of this novel's author. A 1902 pamphlet by Lenin is named after this novel. Name this novel by Nikolai Chernyshevsky.

This author wrote about Magin traveling to Karsovy to search for his brother in the short story "In a Northern Country." She punningly riffed on the title phrase of her short story "A Mown Lawn," and wrote about a fickle man in "Sketches for a Life of Wassilly." An unnamed narrator tries to organize her memories of a failed love affair into a novel in this author's only novel, The End of the Story. Before marrying Siri Hustvedt, Paul Auster was married to this author. She is also known for her translations of French novels, including Swann's Way and Madame Bovary, but she is best known for her short stories, collections of which include Break It Down, Samuel Johnson Is Indignant, and Varieties of Disturbance. Name this American author whose Collected Stories were published in 2009, and who shares her surname with the author of "Life in the Iron Mills."

The author of this essay is apprehensive of a framed verse beginning "God bless the corners of this house" because it is the kind of ironic detail that would be mentioned in the news if a violent crime ever took place in the house. This essay includes an excerpt from a psychiatric report about an attack of vertigo and nausea suffered by the author. The author of this essay recalls sitting on the floor in a recording studio while three members of The Doors are waiting for Jim Morrison to arrive. This essay chronicles Huey Newton's arrest for the murder of John Frey, and its author interviews Linda Kasabian, one of the key witnesses in the Tate-LaBianca murder trial. A volume collecting the nonfiction of this essay's author gets its title from its opening line, "We tell ourselves stories in order to live." name this Joan Didion essay named for a Beatles album.

Undoubtedly the most famous Canadian example of this genre is about atomic bomb testing in Polynesia; that work is Laurence Hyde's Southern Cross. One work in this genre is about a slave trader who kills an African and steals his drum, and is called Madman's Drum. Another work in this genre follows a generic man's trip through a city, after which he enters a forest and dies, whereupon his soul leaves his body and stomps on his heart. The pioneers of this genre included Otto Nückel and the author of The Idea and Passionate Journey, Frans Masereel. This genre was introduced to America by the author of such works as Wild Pilgrimage and Gods' Man, Lynd Ward. Name this genre of proto-graphic novels with no text, which was popular among the German Expressionists.

Each stanza of one of this man's early poems ends with the refrain "Through two points only one straight line can pass." His first work to be translated into English was the novel Not of This Time, Not of This Place. In a long autobiographical poem by this author, the speaker is an old man who reflects on his life, comparing it to the travels of Benjamin of Tudela. A poem which notes that "I wasn't one of the six million who died in the Shoah" also contains a line which provides the title of his collection Open Closed Open, and his other collections in English include Exile at Home and a volume of selected poems translated by Ted Hughes. Some of poems refer to a friend of his who died in the Holocaust as "little Ruth." An early poem by him is named after Yehuda Ha-Levi, who shares his first name. Name this 20th-century Israeli poet.

One of this poet's works contains a faux-Latin poem attributed to Ovid called "Kettelopotomachia" or "battle of the kettle and the pot." In another poem, he wrote that "Once to every man and nation comes the moment to decide, in the strife of Truth with Falsehood, for the good or evil side." In a poem inspired by the death of his daughter Blanche, he described telling his daughter Mabel that the Lord is responsible for making snow fall. This author of "The Present Crisis" and "The First Snowfall" also wrote a work whose title character, Hosea, is contrasted with Birdofredum Sawin. The year 1848 saw the publication of his most important long works, including The Vision of Sir Launfal, The Biglow Papers, and a work which satirized Margaret Fuller and other literary figures of the age. Name this author of A Fable for Critics.

Identify the following works of Russian author Mikhail Bulgakov F15PE. A. A scientist transplants human testicles and a pituitary gland in a dog which, resultantly, becomes more and more human. A lecherous, drunken debaucher, the dog, whose name is Sharik, eventually becomes an official in the Soviet government.

In one section of this book, the author discusses the post-court-martial scene in The Caine Mutiny, deploring Wouk's treatment of the mutineers. The author also argues against the collective nature of the "creative vehicle" in part five's section on "The Fight Against Genius." Containing such sections as "Inconspicuous Consumption" and "The Web of Friendship," the final chapter examines the title figure "At Home." It includes an appendix on how to cheat on personality tests and begins with a discussion of the title figure's ideology, describing the decline of the protestant ethic as the result of corporate forces. FTP, identify this 1956 work which decries the conformity of corporate employees, written by William Whyte.

It features the proud father Old Gudaal and the Prince, who pursues his lost love on a gallant steed. When the Georgian noble's daughter awakens she can only remember clear dreams, sad eyes, and tender words. Though a messenger tries to sway the title character, he replies, "You are no judge of such as we/ For her heart belongs to me." Begun when its author was sixteen, it was reworked numerous times, most notably after his exile to the Caucasus. Subtitled, "An Eastern Tale," it climaxes with a kiss between the aforementioned Tamara, who is instantly killed, and the title figure who opens the poem by flying over the earth and contemplating his exile from heaven. Identify this long poem about a former angel by Lermontov

In a novel of this title, Marcelo Desnoyers immigrates to Argentina and helps Julio Madriaga found a ranch. The namesakes of that novel are alluded to in the sixth chapters of both Zechariah, where they emerge from mountains of brass, and coincidently the sixth chapter of another Biblical book. The translations of the two passages are debated, particularly the appropriateness of adjectives like dapple, bay, or grizzled. In the second appearance the Greek word 'chloros' is used. Though it literally means green, typically the adjective pale is used to describe the group's final member. For 10 points-- who is this quartet of figures traditionally associated with War, Famine, Pestilence, and Death and found in the Book of Revelation.

Based loosely on John Milius, this character borrows from Shakespeare's Hamlet when he ends a eulogy with the words "Goodnight sweet Prince". In the edited-for-TV version of the film he can be heard to exclaim the words "when you meet a stranger in the Alps" and "when you fix a stranger scrambled eggs" while he employs a strange interrogation tactic. He demonstrates knowledge of the works of Sholom Aleichem to attest to being Jewish, a faith he was a convert to. This owner of a private security firm also speaks about Constitutional law when he admonishes a waitress with the Supreme Court's views of "prior restraint" of free speech. Later he hurls a bowling ball at Uli Kunkle, the man from the beaver picture. Name this character who gave us the lines "Eight year olds" and "Chinaman is not the preferred nomenclature" as the sidekick to "The Dude" in The Big Lebowski.

An elaborate hoax involves passing Snawley off as another figure's father. Persons like Miss La Creevy, a miniaturist, and Mrs. Wititterley, a hypochondriac, provide employment and shelter to one of the main characters who is harassed by Mr. Mantalini. A more sinister figure is Lord Verisopht who dies in a duel. The third of its author's novels, it was begun after he and his friend Hablot Browne traveled to Yorkshire to investigate certain institutions firsthand. Presumably this experience led to the creation of Dotheboys Academy, run by an evil schoolmaster. Identify this work that features such memorable characters as Smike, the Cheerybles, and Wackford Squeers, a novel by Charles Dickens.
The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby

Minor characters in this work include the alcoholic Romola Martin, who still lives in Iowa and is introduced in a flashback, as well as the imperious janitor, Mrs. Johnson. The latter takes it upon herself to organize a lavish funeral midway through the novel, for a failed vaudeville clown named Harry. That ceremony attracts numerous members of the San Bernardino Arms community including the dwarf Abe Kusich. Early on in the novel we meet Earle Shoop, a cowboy from Arizona, who dates the actress Faye for part of the story. The novel ends with a mob scene in front of Kahn's Persian Palace, where the childlike Homer Simpson has hit a child. Identify this novel that ends with a vision of the painting, "The Burning of Los Angeles," by its protagonist Tod Hackett, a work by Nathanel West.

He wrote a four line work about a "tusky boar" called "Caradoc" as well as a couplet comparing the "thrush" to the "wood lark." Prose works by him include the critical "Some Remarks on the Poems of John Lydgate" and an "Essay on Norman Architecture." He completed some lines on "the ghost of John Dennis" and his lesser known odes include works on some "Fatal Sisters," "The Descent of Odin," and "The Bard." This author of a Sonnet on the death of his friend, Richard West, is better known for another pair of Odes: one on "a distant prospect of Eton College" and the other on "the Death of a Favorite Cat" who had an accident. Identify this British poet best known for a 1751 poem that begins "The curfew tolls the knell of parting day," a work known as "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard."

At one point men meet at Moloney Street to discuss the UPU's involvement in the conflict that dominates the beginning and end of this work. Earlier Peter and Bill Green share a Heineken and discuss the effects of climate on moral character. After he finds out that his osu girlfriend is pregnant, its protagonist borrows money from Sam to get Clara an abortion. Soon after this occurs he loses his mother Hannah and decided to give up his ideals and start taking bribes. The novel begins and ends with a trial for corruption in Lagos and is essentially a sequel to Things Fall Apart. Identify this 1960 work about the life of Obi Okonkwo by Chinua Achebe.

An unnamed narrator tries to save the title character from torture in "The Foreigner." A man learns how to play an instrument in a fortnight to avoid the firing squad in "The Three Key Bugle." A pact between Death and Suicide is depicted in a novel that imagines the year 2316 in The Strange Friend of Tito Gil. In a better known novel, Angustias risks her life to save a wounded army officer who recovers and berates her, but ultimately falls in love with her. That work, Captain Poison, was finished after his first works: The Finale of Norma and Diary of a Witness of the War of Africa. His greatest novel takes place in Andalusia and deals with the rivalry between a "Corregidor" and a miller for the latter's wife. Identify this author of The Three Cornered Hat.
Juan Ruiz de Alarcon y Mendoza

Modeled on an incident that happened to Mary Doherty, this work was the subject of Robert Penn Warren's essay "Irony with a Center." Its title refers to the protagonist's terrifying dream during which she eats portions of the namesake object and is haunted by her onetime suitor. Originally published in Hound and Horn magazine, it later served as the title to a collection of its author's stories that included "Magic" and "Maria Concepcion." The title character is repulsed by the charismatic Braggioni, who sings to her bawdily as the story opens, and feels regret that she betrayed and facilitated the death of a man who may have loved her named Eugenio. Identify this short story, set during the Obregon revolution, that focuses on a young gringa named Laura and was written by Katherine Anne Porter.

He theorized that limiting one's options ahead of time was a way to achieve better ends, an idea known as precommitment. His attempts to quit smoking led to related work on addiction, arguing that self control is a more valuable determinant of happiness than wealth. In a 1997 Foreign Affairs article, he argued that the costs of fighting global warming were overestimated, while in papers like "The Mind as Consuming Organ", he pioneered behavioral economics. He is also known for his model of segregation, which showed that a neighborhood can be segregated even if no individuals prefer it. His best known work, however, was in the paradox of nuclear deterrence and his game theoretic book, The Strategy of Conflict. FTP, identify this Harvard economist, winner of the 2005 Nobel Prize in economics.

One chapter opens with a description of Carlisle Street in Johnstown, while another chapter compares Dougherty County to a place where "the winged ram Chrysomallus" was robbed of its wool. That latter chapter, "Of the Quest of the Golden Fleece," makes mention of the Sam Hose affair, and the author explores musical works such as "March On" and "Steal Away" in its final chapter. Its third chapter lambastes another thinker for his "triple paradox" of "adjustment and submission," and it uses the metaphor of a veil to illustrate the "invisibility" of a group of people the author feels are bereft of certain rights. Beginning with the statement that the "problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color line," name this book that seeks to sketch the "spiritual world" of African-Americans, written by W.E.B DuBois.

This novel includes descriptions of a dice game for the hand of a harlot as well as the dissection of Francesco. It also describes the creation of machines of war by the visitor Bernardo. The title character later participates in a campaign against Il Toro and the House of Montanza. But when peace is finally declared, he helps to recapture the advantage by poisoning all of his master's enemies, including the Prince's best friend, Don Riccardo, at a banquet. By the end of the novel, he is sent to the dungeon for killing the Princess. It begins with the title character revealing that he strangled his predecessor, Jehoshaphat, who had been a buffoon and had given his kind a bad name. Identify this 1944 work about a malevolent 26 inch man, the masterpiece of Par Lagerkvist.

The protagonist of this novel attempts to help Madame Dandelard, an Italian woman fleeing from her abusive husband. Later, he watches Madame Alboni in a performance of Don Giovanni while sharing a box with the chatty Dora. The protagonist's friends include the boorish Mr. Tristram, who thinks the paintings in the Louvre are for sale, and Valentin, who dies in a duel in Switzerland for the hand of Mademoiselle Nioche. The English servant Mrs. Bread possesses a letter proving that Madame de Bellegarde murdered her husband, but the letter does not enable the title character to marry Claire de Cintre, who becomes a nun. Name this Henry James novel centering on Christopher Newman, an expatriate in France.

This man's works for piano includes the posthumously published Souvenirs of Bayreuth. His choral works include Caligula and The Birth of Venus, and like Rameau, he published a Treatise on Harmony. In addition to writing the Cantique de Jean Racine and a Missa Brevis for female voices, he wrote incidental music to Pellias and Mellisande and a one-act divertissement called Masques et Bergamasques. His operas Prometheus and Penelope are seldom performed, but he gained renown with such works as L'horizon chimerique and La bonne chanson. FTP, name this master of the song cycle and teacher of Ravel and Les Six, perhaps best known for an 1890 Requiem composed after the death of his father.

Parson Welldo compares the antagonist to a basilisk in the last scene of this play, whose epigraph features sonnets dedicated "To the Ingenious Author," by Henry Moody and Thomas Jay. Other characters include the servants Amble and Furnace, as well as Greedy, a "hungry justice of the peace." The alehouse-keeper Tapwell and his wife Froth refuse to give beer to the protagonist, who is aided by Jack Marrall in a plot to steal the deed to an estate. Margaret ultimately marries Tom, the stepson of Lady Allworth, despite ostensibly being courted by Lord Lovell. Meanwhile, the prodigal hero outwits his miserly uncle, the evil Sir Giles Overreach. Name this comedy in which Frank Wellborn overcomes his financial obligations, a work by Philip Massinger.
A New Way to Pay Old Debts

This author wrote an unfinished story entitled "Lulu and His Wife," as well as a poem beginning with an epigraph from Pilgrim's Progress in which a bird remarks that "the air was like marble." This author's translations from Portuguese include "Three Stories by Clarice Lispector" and The Diary of Helena Morley, while works like "Over 2,000 Illustrations and a Complete Concordance" and "The Bight" can be found in A Cold Spring. This writer claimed "The art of losing isn't hard to master" in "One Art," and took the identity of a seven-year-old listening to her Aunt Consuelo's screams in "In the Waiting Room." Those two works, along with the poems "The End of March," "The Moose," and "Crusoe in England," are featured in her compilation Geography III. Name this student of Marianne Moore, and author of the collections Questions of Travel and North and South.

The one entitled "The Lay of Ike" states that the title character "misread even Clausewitz" and had a "wide empty grin that never lost a vote." In "A Stimulant for an Old Beast," the speaker states that "Rilke was a jerk." Eleven are dedicated to Delmore Schwartz and some were published in the author's collection His Toy, His Dream, His Rest. In the three hundred and eighty fourth, the main character spits on his father's grave for committing suicide and expresses a desire to run an ax through the corpse, and they also include "A Strut for Roethke" and "‘The Prisoner of Shark Island' with Paul Muni". Focusing on a teacher who has a minstrel show alter ego named Mr. Bones, identify this group of poems about Mr. Henry by John Berryman.

Originally located in the Alabaster Chamber, it is believed that Dosso Dossi altered this work in order for it to be better displayed alongside his Aeneas and Achates on the Libyan Coast. The female characters in this painting were at one time more modestly dressed, though the pheasant on the upper right remains from the original landscape. Fruits can be seen on the ground and bowls are passed around. Silvanus is depicted with a wreath of pine needles, while an unidentified female holds a quince fruit, and Priapus advances on the nymph Lotis. Commissioned by Alfonso D'Este, it was begun by Giovanni Bellini, but finished by his, then, student Titian, identify this painting depicting deities engaging in revelry.

One of the main characters of this novel describes how her Uncle Lewis was disinherited after buying seemingly worthless Giotto paintings, and the title character once told Leland Stanford to write a check for seventy five million dollars to the federal government as payment for stolen public lands. This work describes General Fierro's killing of three hundred prisoners who were offered a chance to escape, and Innocenco Mansalvo prophesizes that the title character has come to Mexico looking for death. Focusing on a love triangle between General Arroyo, who serves in Pancho Villa's army, Harriet Winslow, and the title character, for 10 points name this novel about Ambrose Bierce who is given the title epithet, a work by Carlos Fuentes.

In this work, Ariphron's failed attempt to mentor Cleinias is mentioned, and Prodicus' habit of mincing words such as "will" and "wish" is parodied. A question about the appropriate length of responses to questions nearly derails this work's central debate, and Hippias' offer to recite a poem is declined. The meaning of a poem by Simonides is discussed in this work, and the meeting of the two central characters is sparked by Socrates' concern about the education of Hippocrates. Beginning with Socrates abandoning his attempts to seduce Alcibiades and focusing on the question of whether virtue can be taught, for 10 points name this dialogue in which Socrates debates the title sophist.

His 1848 collection of poems contains such works as "To the Dandelion", "An Indian Summer Reverie" and "The Changeling", and his Conversations of Some Old Poets calls for the abolition of slavery. His collection Among My Books contains a series of essays on literary figures, and his wife Maria White inspired the poems in his A Year's Life. His final collection Heartsease and Rue contains an elegy to Agassiz, and characters he invented include Sir Launfel and Reverend Wilbur. The poet of the "Commemoration Ode", for 10 points name this author of The Biglow Papers.

A 1991 book with 59 entries by computer scientist Don Knuth (ka-nooth) was based on his series of MIT lectures given on this topic. It is acknowledged by an inscription used on the cups at In-N-Out Burger and was the subject of a Boston Red Sox joke on the Family guy. The larger section of which it is part is centered on a conversation with the Pharisee Nicodemus, who asks "How can a man be born when he is old?" This man's first wife Paccia Marciana quickly died and he bestowed the rather unique title of mater castrorum on his second wife. Famous for his unique birthplace of Lepcis Magna in Libya, name this Roman emperor from 193-211 A.D., the father of Geta and Caracalla.

Its protagonists meet such figures as the blind guitarist Homer and the three young ladies with the last name Muse. In one of them a young man throws a stone at a blackbird who told him to lie down. Another piece notes that when the narrator was in love, then he was "clean and brave." Identify this author of A First Love, A Month in the Country, Sportsmen's Sketches, and Fathers and Sons.

One of the first critics to take genre fiction seriously, he sang the praises of Henry James' tale "The Other House" in his The Delights of Detection. The poems "Stella," "The Last Words," and the opening work "Nox," are angry poems that contrast dramatically with a collection he wrote late in life on the island of Serk, Songs of the Streets and the Woods. He wrote of "melodious multitudes" that strove to lure Apollo from his "impregnable domain" in one poem, and expressed a desire to learn more about Ucalegon and Melchizedek in another. Written in a characteristic fourteen-line stanza of iambic tetrameter with alternating feminine and masculine rhymes, this work's early plot is set in motion when writing materials are borrowed from the nurse Filipyevna. Talbot Potter is the main character of his Harlequin and Columbine, while the novel Cherry satirizes academic life. A vision attributed to "a poor woman of Laon" imagined this man's friend Count Bego drinking molten gold, his wife Ermengard weighed down with great boulders, and his own name written out of paradise after his complicity in the killing of his nephew Bernard of Italy. Popular movies were made of The Russia House and The Spy Who Came in from the Cold and Alec Guinness has repeatedly played the main hero of, what British novelist of the Cold War most famous for creating George Smiley?

Ultimately Horner's efforts to woo the title character, Margery, succeed. Identify this play by William Wycherley about Mr. Pinchwife who is cuckolded by a rural female spouse?

His prose included the letters of a character named "Robert Slender" and a series of stories about a defrocked priest named Hezekiah Salem. His poem "To Sir Toby" decried the treatment of slaves on a plantation, where he had worked as a secretary, while his "On the Religion of Nature" revised the views expressed in his darkly comic poem "Pestilence," about the yellow fever outbreak. At Princeton, he co-authored Father Bombo's Pilgrimage to Mecca in Arabia and "On the Rising Glory of America," with Hugh Henry Brackenridge. But he is best known for his political writing at The National Gazette and for poems describing the beauty of a flower's short life and the solemnity of a native cemetery. Name this "Poet of the American Revolution" who wrote "The Wild Honey Suckle" and "The Indian Burying Ground."

Charles Philipon was prosecuted for a scandalous caricature of this man's transformation into a pear, which was then used as a symbol of sedition in works by Flaubert and Stendhal. Years earlier, as a subordinate of Charles-Francois Dumouriez, he received credit for the victory at Jemappes and was denounced for treason following the disaster at Neerwinden, forcing him to flee to America. Becoming rich after marrying the daughter of the King of the Two Sicilies, he still sent his children to public schools and continued using the surname Egalité, and was hence well positioned when the July Revolution overthrew Charles X. FTP, name this Citizen-King of France.

One of the works that lays out this problem includes a comparison between one group's inclination to put roosters that lay eggs on trial and another groups interpretation of such roosters as omens. This problem's namesake wrote a work on it called The Grand Titration. One answer to part of this problem is Mark Elvin's high-level equilibrium trap, which proposes that high population densities prohibit centralization and productivity increases. The namesake of this conundrum is the subject of a Simon Winchester biography titled after his "love." Its namesake tried to answer this question in part by noting how in some lineages of thought, natural law and natural science have a common origin. This quandary's namesake, a British biochemist, ran a Science Co- operation Office in Chongqing. Name this question that asks why despite having an initial technological advantage, China fell behind the west in science for hundreds of years.

The durability of these tools were greatly improved thanks to Robert Randsome's work in the 18th century. William Seward claimed that "no man has been as inadequately rewarded" as Jethro Wood, who introduced a relatively modern design of this tool. In the Middle Ages, the Mediterranean scratch example of these tools was replaced by a "heavy" one in Germany, thus decreasing the need for the cross usage of these. Thomas Jefferson designed a mouldboard "of least resistance" for use in one of these tools. Common components of these include the coulter and the share. Steel was introduced into the construction of these by John Deere. Name these devices that are used to breakup and turn the soil.

This author of Four Distressed Poems compared the heavens to a hen's egg. His other literary contributions include a poem in which a river is one of the title "four sorrows" that keep him from a woman and the introduction of a literary style of hypothetical discourse called shelun in a work about his idleness. This man reinvented a contraption consisting of a man like figure on a cart that would always point south. He's not Archimedes, but he did independently invent the odometer. He was the first to use water to run an armillary sphere, allowing for better astronomical predictions. One of his devices had eight noisemaking sculpted frogs that would catch copper balls that fell from dragon heads. For 15 points, name this Han dynasty inventor of a seismometer.

In one of this author's novels, the drunken Knopf urinates on the titular object which is owned by the firm of Heinrich Kroll which also employs the protagonist who falls in love with a schizophrenic girl who calls herself Isabelle. In addition to that novel about Ludwig Bodmer, he wrote a novel in which the paralyzed Joan Madou is given a fatal injection by her lover Ravic. This author of The Black Obelisk and Arch of Triumph wrote of a man who gives away his passports which his wife Helen and he had planned to use to escape to the United States in his novel about Josef Schwarz, The Night in Lisbon. In another work, the protagonist spends a night pinned down by the body of a French soldier he stabs and beats Corporal Himmelstoss. FTP, name this author of The Road Back who described Kemmerich, Muller, and Paul Baumer in All Quiet on the Western Front.

One poem by this man asks "Where is the Christopher Columbus to whom is owed the / forgetting of a continent" and declares "We are going farther without ever advancing", and another of his poem's states "The Octoroons sing songs of dying / To their chestnut colored wives" and begins "The yellow fades from red to green". In a novella, this author described the rise to fame and subsequent murder by a mob of Croniamantal. The author of Always, Windows, and The Poet Assassinated also wrote a poem which states "The most modern European is you Pope Pius X" and begins "You are tired at last of this old world / O shepherd Eiffel Tower the flock of bridges bleats at the morning", Zone. In one play by this author, the title character's husband gives birth to 40,000 children in one afternoon after she abandons him and becomes a general. FTP, name this French author of the poetry collections Calligrammes and Alcools as well as the play The Breasts of Tiresias.

In one work by this man, Darry Berrill swaps jobs with his wife and is joined in trashing the household by Barry Derrill, and in another, Jerry attempts to help his drunken coworker Sammy sign a postal order for the titular amount of money. The prostitute Jannice dies making the sign of the cross and is pursued by The Dreamer in another of his works. This author of the one-act plays The End of the Beginning and A Pound on Demand and the morality play Within the Gates wrote a play which ends with Cyril Poges climbing to the roof of his flooding house and another play in which Minnie Powell dies hiding bombs and Donal Davoren pretends to be the titular figure. His other plays include one in which Teddy Foran is blinded and Barney is caught removing the dress of Jessie Taite, the one-time girlfriend of soccer star Harry Heegan and one in which Johnny is killed for informing on Robbie Tancred and Jack Boyle is abandoned by his wife. FTP, name this playwright of Purple Dust, The Shadow of a Gunman, The Silver Tassie, and Juno and the Paycock.

The opening scene of this work describes a fifteen or twenty foot high smooth mass of granite after the narrator describes the national significance of Lovell's Flight. After being brought to safety, the protagonist is too sick to speak, and several days pass, making it too late for him to tell the others where his wounded friend is. After marrying that friend's daughter Dorcas, the protagonist takes over that friend's farm but cannot focus properly due to his overwhelming guilt and is forced to sell it. While traveling in the wilderness, Cyrus is accidentally shot by his father Reuben Bourne on the exact spot where the title character died. FTP, name this short story in which the title character is never properly put to rest, a work of Nathaniel Hawthorne.

One poem by this author states "How dare anyone object / Tell me I had better not exist" and declares that gold chains are found in "mines in South Africa / Where our brothers sweat their lives underground". In one work of this author, wealthy Paul H. And his family are murdered by the poor yard worker Christopher, and another follows a character who owns a string of hotels in San Francisco used as sanctuaries for runaway slaves and plans to join John Brown's raid on Harper's Ferry. In addition to that novel about Annie and Mary Ellen Pleasant, one of this author's characters reminisces about her parents Boy and Kitty through flashbacks while on a truck with guerrillas before they are ambushed. FTP, name this author of Free Enterprise who wrote about Clare Savage in Abeng and No Telephone to Heaven.

One character in this work discourages a group of lumberjacks from drinking to their friend's death in an attempt to hide that he already drank the entire barrel of brandy, and when that character is refused brandy by Mjurk, he causes a riot in the Night Cloud café by singing a dirty song. After one character in this work claims he cannot seduce his fiancée due to her innocence, another character approves of his decision and promptly seduces her, leading to her drowning herself in a river. In addition to Johanna Reiher, the protagonist abandons his lover Sophie Barger and stabs his friend Eckart in a barfight. FTP, name this play following the titular womanizing poet, a work of Bertolt Brecht.

This man declares "Speed is violence / Power is violence / Weight is violence" in his poem Butterfly, and another instructs the addressee to "take care…lest you become / a dancer disinherited in mid-dance". A schoolmaster controversially fences off a footpath in one of this man's short stories, and Jonathan preserves his bicycle by burying it in his yard in another. Those two stories, "Dead Men's Path" and "Civil Peace", were published in his collection Girls at War. In one of his novels, Ikem is assassinated by his dictator- friend Sam, and in another, Oduche converts to Christianity, angering his father Ezeulu. FTP, name this man who wrote about Obi's arrest for bribery and the exile and suicide of Okonkwo in No Longer at Ease and Things Fall Apart.

One character in this work travels to a village fair to sell cakes shaped like Gothic ornaments, and another character journeys in the rain to meet his old love when his wife refuses to contact her. As a boy, the protagonist works in the bakery of his great grandaunt Drusilla and admires his schoolmaster who sends him texts while studying for a degree in Christminster, Richard Phillotson. Two of the protagonist's children are hanged by his son by his first wife, Little Father Time, after a harsh remark is made by his pregnant wife Sue Bridehead, and the protagonist takes to drinking after twice being tricked into marriage by Arabella Donn. FTP, name this work about the stonemason Fawley, the final novel of Thomas Hardy.

In one work by this author, rocks from the titular location are converted to earth and a writer is the only character who can hear the native creatures, and in another, the title character is drowned in a bathtub by the maid and discusses the possibility of making war on the ants. In addition to Poet on the Moon and The Fate of a Cockroach, the title character is executed by dictators who attempt to take the apple of peace from him in his play Angels' Prayer. In another play, the Detective believes that Bihana's body was used to nourish an orange tree after she was killed by her husband Bahadir. His other plays include one following the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus and one in which a Mamluk ruler is revealed to legally be a slave. FTP, name this playwright of The Tree Climber, The People of the Cave, and The Sultan's Dilemma.
